name: Limi dialect of Humla Bhotia
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Wilde, Christopher Pekka. 2001. Preliminary phonological analysis of the Limi dialect of Humla Bhotia. MA thesis, General Linguistics, University of Helsinki. 91 pp. (Helda handle 10138/19353; Glottolog ref 81810.)
catalog_locator: Sec. 8.6.3 'Stress placement or tone spread?', pp. 61-64: quoted sentences p. 62, p. 63, p. 64; sec. 8.8 'Conclusions and residue' p. 65; tone-bearing unit sec. 6.2 pp. 33-34; disyllabic pitch patterns sec. 8.6.2 pp. 59-60.
catalog_quote: In monosyllabic morphemes in Limi there is a simple pitch contrast between a rising contour and a level/falling contour. In disyllabic morphemes it is possible that the contrast is more a question of stress placement. In disyllabic words, the syllable with possible stress (that is, the one with higher pitch) does not necessarily have a lengthened vowel nucleus nor do changes occur in the quality of the vowel nucleus of this syllable. There only seems to be a minimal difference in intensity between high pitched (stressed) syllables and low(er) pitched (non-stressed) syllables. In fact, in some instances it seems that the intensity of a syllable with lower pitch may have the same or even a greater intensity than a syllable with high pitch. This observation is based solely on my impression; more accurate acoustic analysis is imperative in order to clarify the matter. [p. 62] ... As stated in Section 6.2. the tone-bearing unit of the word in Limi is the morpheme. ... Thus the LM –pitch pattern which is found on the disyllabic words of the form [cv̀cv́] would be a natural outcome of tone spread. [p. 63] ... At this stage I am unable to discuss the issue of stress in further detail. [p. 64] ... The following contrastive prosodic features have been found in Limi: /length/, /nasalisation/, /tense/, /lax/, /rising tone/ and /falling or level tone/. [p. 65]
world_status: statement found in an open source

In monosyllabic morphemes in Limi there is a simple pitch contrast between a rising contour and a level/falling contour. In disyllabic morphemes it is possible that the contrast is more a question of stress placement. In disyllabic words, the syllable with possible stress (that is, the one with higher pitch) does not necessarily have a lengthened vowel nucleus nor do changes occur in the quality of the vowel…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Limi (Humla) is described as a register-tone language: contrastive tense/lax phonation plus two tonemes, /rising/ vs /falling-or-level/, with the morpheme as tone-bearing unit (p. 66; pp. 33-34). Disyllabic morphemes show two pitch patterns, low-high [cv$cv@] (rising toneme spread) and level [cvcv]. Wilde explicitly raises the alternative that these are second-syllable vs first-syllable stress (/ÿHOˈpŒ/ 'belly' vs /ˈle¤pŒ/ 'brain', p. 63) but finds no length or vowel-quality correlate and only minimal intensity differences, and leaves stress unresolved. No fixed stress position is asserted; if stress exists it would be lexically tied to the tone class (final in rising-tone words, initial in level-tone words).
new_statements.exceptions: Pitch of the second syllable in level-pattern words varies freely or by speaker, and low-pitched suffixes are excluded (8.6.1-8.6.2); the epenthetic vowel [Î/«] tends to fall on the non-prominent syllable but lax phonation also produces it (p. 63). Author cites Kagate (Hoehlig et al. 1976: 'main stress is usually on the first syllable') and Sherpa (Gordon 1970: stress placement significant in disyllables) as comparanda, not as claims about Limi.
new_statements.domain_note: Disyllabic morphemes (not polymorphemic words: 'in polymorphemes tone does not spread over morpheme boundaries', p. 34) elicited in isolation and checked in sentential context; the (a)/(b) opposition is retained in sentences. Sentence intonation: default lowering on the final 1-2 syllables (8.7, p. 64).
new_statements.identity_note: Wilde 2001 describes specifically the Limi dialect of Humla Bhotia (Limi valley, Humla District; speakers interviewed in Kathmandu), one of five dialects he names (Limi, Upper Humla, La Yakhba, Nyinba, Humli Khyampa). Glottolog maps 'Limi = Humla [hut]' (huml1238) and lists no separate Limi languoid; do not confuse with limi1243 (Limi, a Central Ngwi language of Yunnan). de Vries 2014 covers the Dojam/Bargaun/Hepka varieties of the same [hut].

sources.note: Whole thesis is a phonology. Ch. 6-8 treat prosody: Limi has contrastive /length/, /nasalisation/, /tense/ vs /lax/ phonation and two tonemes /rising/ vs /falling-or-level/ (p. 66); tone-bearing unit = the morpheme, a rising tone spreads over a disyllable as low-then-mid pitch (pp. 33-34). Sec. 8.6.3 'Stress placement or tone spread?' (pp. 61-64) asks whether the two disyllabic pitch patterns [cv$cv@] (LM) vs [cvcv] (level) are really second- vs first-syllable stress; Wilde finds no vowel lengthening or quality change and only minimal, impressionistic intensity differences, notes the epenthet…

sources.note: Nothing on stress; confirms Wilde 2001 is the only descriptive (phonology) reference for [hut]; other references are Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 (subclassification comment) and Moseley 2010 (endangerment). Alternative names: Dangali, Humla 'Bhotia', Phoke; 'Limirong Tibetan' in UNESCO.
